feedback: When a learner says a square is 'too square' to be a rectangle, walk the rectangle checklist together item by item; if it passes every test, the square belongs in the 'rectangle' ring without leaving 'square'.

If a learner thinks a rectangle must have two long and two short sides, show a run of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square, confirming each passes the same tests — length is not a defining property.

If a learner accepts the shared properties yet still won't let one shape be in two categories, offer everyday inclusion analogies (a spaniel is a dog AND an animal at once) and more nested-set practice rather than drilling the yes/no fact.
Reinforce justification: the point is naming the shared properties ('four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel'), not the bare yes/no answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Category membership is decided by which property tests a shape passes, not by how it looks; a square passes every rectangle test, so a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) — and one shape can belong to two nested categories at once.
learnerActions: Take a plain quadrilateral and adjust its corners until all four angles are right angles (check with a set-square); confirm whether opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Run the rectangle checklist item by item — '4 right angles? ✓ opposite sides equal and parallel? ✓' — and place the shape inside the 'rectangle' ring of a nested diagram when it passes all tests.

Now, starting from a rectangle with all four sides equal (a square), pull one pair of opposite sides longer while keeping all four right angles, so the shape stays a rectangle but is no longer a square; then shorten them, still keeping the right angles, until all four sides are equal again and watch it move into the innermost 'square' region nested inside 'rectangle', which is nested inside 'quadrilateral'.
Say out loud, in your own words, why the SAME shape can sit in two boxes at once ('it is a rectangle because... and also a square because...').
Repeat with a rhombus checklist to see the square also sits inside 'rhombus' where the rings overlap.
activities.title: Sort and stretch: does the shape pass the rectangle tests?

feedback: A correct answer is 'yes — a square is a rectangle: it has four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel, plus its four sides happen to be equal, so it is a special rectangle.'
If a learner judges by appearance ('it's too square-looking') and cannot state the defining properties, build the checklist together and test item by item.
For 'a square turned 45° is a diamond', confirm turning a shape does not change which property tests it passes, so it is still a square and still a rectangle.

When asked to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle, the learner should discover this is impossible: every square passes all the rectangle tests, so no such shape exists — whereas a rectangle that is not a square CAN be drawn. Noticing this one-way asymmetry is the sign of real property-based understanding.
Treat 'it can be a square OR a rectangle but not both' as a maturing class-inclusion stage, not a false fact; give more nested-set experience rather than correction drills.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before testing exposes prototype thinking; reconciling a 'no, too square' prediction with the square passing every rectangle test is where the concept takes hold. The asymmetry — you can draw a rectangle that is not a square, but not a square that is not a rectangle — is the tell of genuine understanding.
learnerActions: Before testing, predict whether a square 'counts as' a rectangle and say WHY.
Check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler: four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel?
If the result differs from your prediction, explain what changed your mind.

Answer probing questions: Does it matter how long the sides are? Is a square turned to look like a diamond still a square and still a rectangle? Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?
Decide whether a square is also a special rhombus, and justify.
activities.title: Predict, test, explain with a real square

feedback: Accept a non-example only when the learner shows a defining property is missing for each category it must be excluded from. Some missing properties exclude only some categories: 'no right angles → not a rectangle or square' still leaves rhombus open, so also check 'the four sides are not all equal → not a rhombus or square'. One missing property can exclude all three: rectangles, rhombuses and squares all have both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so a shape without two pairs of parallel sides (e.g. a kite or trapezium) is none of them.
Accept the inclusion claim only when the learner cites the defining properties the square passes, not just that 'it looks like one' or 'both have four sides'.
If a learner cannot produce a non-prototypical rectangle, offer tilted and nearly-square examples and have them verify each against the checklist.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning about which properties are ABSENT (for non-examples) and which are PRESENT (for inclusion) consolidates definition-based classification and loosens the oblong prototype.
learnerActions: Draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, and say which defining property it is missing for EACH of those three categories.
Draw a rectangle that is not a square.
Explain to a sceptical 'shape detective' why a square still counts as a rectangle even though it doesn't look like a long oblong, citing the defining properties it passes.
Sort a mixed set of quadrilaterals (including a square, a 45°-tilted rectangle, and a nearly-square rectangle) into a nested/overlapping Venn, justifying each placement by properties.
activities.title: Draw the exceptions and defend the claim
